papers.title: Cas12a Autocatalytic Amplification Coupled with a DNA-Regulated COF Nanozyme Activation for the Colorimetric Detection of Staphylococcus aureus.
papers.abstract: Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is a major foodborne and clinical pathogen, and its rapid and accurate detection are essential for food safety monitoring and clinical diagnostics. Here, we developed a colorimetric platform for quantifying S. aureus that integrates circular DNA (Cir-DNA)-mediated Cas12a autocatalytic amplification with DNA regulation of a covalent organic framework (COFTph-BT) nanozyme. Recognition of the 16S rDNA target by the Cas12a/crRNA complex activates trans-cleavage activity, which linearizes Cir-DNA and initiates an autocatalytic amplification circuit that drives cascade cleavage of probe S1. Signal transduction exploits the differential binding affinities of COFTph-BT for single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) and double-stranded DNA (dsDNA), and its peroxidase activities could be reversely regulated by the surface modification of ssDNA. Cleavage of S1 inhibits its hybridization with COFTph-BT surface-bound S2, maintaining S2 predominantly in its single-stranded form and preserving the catalytic activity of COFTph-BT-S2. The nanozyme subsequently catalyzes the oxidation of colorless 3,3',5,5'-tetramethylbenzidine (TMB) to blue oxidized TMB (oxTMB), generating a colorimetric readout. The assay can be completed within 90 min and achieves a limit of detection (LOD) of 7 CFU mL-1. Integration with smartphone-based image analysis further enables portable colorimetric detection with an LOD of 87 CFU mL-1. This strategy provides an approach for the sensitive colorimetric detection of foodborne pathogens, with potential applications in food safety monitoring and clinical diagnostics.

papers.title: Database resources of the National Center for Biotechnology Information in 2027.
papers.abstract: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) provides biomedical data resources including PubMed®, a repository of citations and abstracts published in life science journals, and ClinicalTrials.gov, a repository of clinical research summaries. NCBI also hosts a multitude of resources providing nucleotide sequences and sequence-derived products, such as proteins and protein structures. Search and retrieval operations are available for most of the 40 distinct repositories, knowledgebases, and services. The E-utilities and NCBI Datasets serve as the programming interface for most of these. Resources receiving significant updates in the past year include PubMed®, PubMed Central® (PMC), SciENcv, ClinicalTrials.gov, ClinVar, dbSNP, dbGaP, GTR, MedGen®, Pathogen Detection and the National Database of Antibiotic Resistant Organisms, and PubChem®. These resources can be accessed through the NCBI home page at https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov.

papers.title: Species-Specific Responses to Snake Fungal Disease: Effects on Space Use, Detection, and Density in Two Semi-Aquatic Natricine Species.
papers.abstract: Wildlife diseases pose increasing threats to reptiles, and evaluating the population-level impacts is often challenging due to the cryptic nature and low detectability of many species. Snake Fungal Disease (SFD or ophidiomycosis), caused by the fungal pathogen Ophidiomyces ophidiicola , has emerged as a potential threat to snake populations, yet few studies have documented population declines directly linked to the disease. We utilized 3 years of passive integrated transponder tag telemetry, disease monitoring, and multi-session spatial capture-recapture models to investigate the effects of snake fungal disease on population densities, spatial scale of detection values, and detection probabilities of Common Watersnake ( Nerodia sipedon ) and Queensnake ( Regina septemvittata ) populations in three central Kentucky streams. We hypothesized that SFD would alter population density over time and that SFD-related physiological impairment or behavioral change would result in species-specific changes in space use and detection probability. Density estimates declined across most sites and sessions over the study period, although these declines were generally not statistically significant, and we could not link them to differences in prevalence rates between sites. Infected N. sipedon exhibited significantly smaller spatial scale of detection values compared to non-infected individuals, whereas no significant differences were observed in R. septemvittata . Infection status did not affect the detection probability of either species, but N. sipedon detection probability increased with day of year, and R. septemvittata detection probability increased with rain accumulation between survey periods. These results indicate that SFD may pose an ongoing risk to snake population stability and can produce sublethal, species-specific effects on space use well before potential population declines and highlight the need for long-term monitoring programs that integrate multiple survey methods and emerging technologies to enhance detection probability and population-level inference.

papers.title: Civilization, assisted reproduction, and the human genome: from relaxed selection to technological correction.
papers.abstract: Assisted reproductive technologies (ART) are now a structural component of reproduction in high-income societies, yet their population-level genetic and clinical consequences remain incompletely characterised. This structured narrative review integrates evolutionary genetics, reproductive epidemiology, ART outcomes, and bioethics. Evidence is strongest for paternal-age-associated de novo mutations, expanded carrier screening (ECS), preimplantation genetic testing for monogenic disorders (PGT-M), and the limitations of testing for polygenic disorders (PGT-P). Moderate, direct but limited adult offspring evidence suggests that intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) used for paternal male-factor infertility can permit intergenerational transmission of infertility-associated phenotypes. ART-associated imprinting and methylation evidence is moderate but confounded by parental subfertility. Repeated donor use may concentrate pathogenic variants; delayed childbearing selection on ovarian reserve and laboratory-derived chemical exposures remain hypothesis-generating. ECS and PGT-M primarily reduce affected pregnancies or births among identified at-risk couples; they do not directly remove carrier alleles or demonstrate a reduction in population mutation load. The population genetic and clinical impact of modern reproduction therefore depends on practice and policy. Coupling ART with ECS, accessible PGT-M and donor governance may reduce preventable inherited disease while preserving reproductive autonomy.

papers.title: Replicon-Based Antiviral Screening Identifies Simeprevir and Mosnodenvir as Inhibitors of Kyasanur Forest Disease Virus.
papers.abstract: Kyasanur Forest Disease virus (KFDV) is an emerging tick-borne flavivirus endemic to India. Currently, molecular studies and antiviral development for KFDV have been hindered by the need for high-containment laboratories to work with the infectious virus and by a lack of simple BSL-2-compatible replicon systems. In this study, we have developed a BSL-2-compatible KFDV sub-genomic replicon that supports viral RNA replication without producing infectious virions. The replicon encodes a Renilla luciferase reporter in place of the structural genes and was stabilized in a bacterial artificial chromosome to overcome plasmid instability associated with flaviviral genomes. Replication competence was validated in BHK-21 cells through luciferase assays, strand-specific RT-PCR, and detection of double-stranded RNA replication intermediates. Using this platform, we screened a panel of anti-flaviviral compounds and identified Ribavirin, Dasabuvir, Simeprevir, and Mosnodenvir as inhibitors of KFDV replication. Dose-response analyses revealed potent antiviral activity for Simeprevir (IC 50 = 4.88 μM) and Mosnodenvir (IC 50 =2.22 μM). Antiviral activity was subsequently confirmed using infectious KFDV, where both compounds reduced viral RNA levels and infectious virus titers. Molecular docking studies suggested distinct mechanisms of inhibition, with Simeprevir potentially acting through allosteric inhibition of NS3 and Mosnodenvir targeting a conserved NS4B binding pocket. Together, these findings establish a robust antiviral screening platform for KFDV and identify promising therapeutics against this emerging pathogen.

papers.title: Diagnostic value and report-anchored antimicrobial prescribing changes following BALF targeted next-generation sequencing in lower respiratory tract infections: a retrospective cohort study.
papers.abstract: Comprehensive evidence on the diagnostic performance and clinical utility of targeted next-generation sequencing (tNGS) in lower respiratory tract infections (LRTIs) remains limited. We evaluated its diagnostic and antimicrobial management value in routine clinical practice. This retrospective cohort study included 433 patients hospitalized with suspected LRTIs at Wuhan First Hospital between February and June 2026. tNGS performance was assessed by pathogen detection profiles, concordance with culture, clinical relevance and antimicrobial prescribing changes within 72 hours of report availability. Within the matched detection spectrum, tNGS detection rate was substantially higher than culture (87.1% vs. 40.2%), with a median of three organisms per report. Higher read counts were associated with a greater likelihood of organism-matched culture positivity. Against the composite clinical adjudication reference, positive tNGS findings had an overall PPV of 89.7%, which was higher for bacterial than fungal detections (92.8% vs. 18.4%). Within 72 h of report availability, 207 patients had regimen modifications; 74.4% were considered mainly or partly supported by tNGS. Among evaluable tNGS-concordant regimens, subsequent AST provided additional support in 69.7%. BALF tNGS broadened microbial detection beyond culture and was associated with early antimicrobial modification. Integrating RPM, culture, AST, and report timing may enhance diagnostic interpretation and clinical actionability.

papers.title: CRC tumor antigens and immune escape: Designing peptide vaccines for colorectal Cancer.
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a leading cause of global cancer mortality, with current therapies often limited by toxicity and resistance. Immunotherapy, particularly peptide-based vaccines, represents a promising alternative by eliciting targeted immune responses. This review provides a critical and comparative synthesis of CRC peptide vaccine development, distinguishing itself from previous reviews by integrating mechanistic insights into immune evasion with a structured framework that connects antigen selection, epitope identification (experimental and computational), and clinical translation. We specifically highlight two underexplored areas: tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs) and the critical distinction between microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) and microsatellite stable (MSS) CRC, which fundamentally dictates mutational burden, neoantigen load, and vaccine responsiveness. We first detail the sophisticated mechanisms of immune evasion employed by CRC, including an immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment enriched with regulatory T cells (Tregs) and myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs), dysregulated antigen presentation via HLA class I alterations, and expression of inhibitory checkpoints. The review critically evaluates methods for epitope identification, contrasting traditional experimental approaches with modern computational strategies that leverage genomics, AI, and immunoinformatics tools for predicting high-affinity, immunogenic epitopes. We emphasize that predicted immunogenicity does not equate to clinical efficacy, and we critically appraise the limitations of current computational tools, including high false-positive rates and poor correlation with in vivo immunogenicity. While promising, challenges remain, including low immunogenicity, human leukocyte antigen (HLA) restriction, and tumor heterogeneity. Future success likely depends on developing multi-epitope, personalized vaccines combined with adjuvants and immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance efficacy. In conclusion, peptide vaccines offer a precise and adaptable platform for CRC immunotherapy, holding significant potential for improving clinical outcomes through targeted immune activation.

papers.title: Preclinical evaluation of an adaptable single-cycle SARS-CoV-2 vaccine against XBB.1.5 in mice and hamsters.
papers.abstract: A next-generation SARS-CoV-2 vaccine must address the currently inadequate prevention of virus transmission, particularly against emerging variants of concern, a challenge that none of the licenced commercial vaccines fully meet. Effective control of respiratory pandemics necessitates vaccines that 1) can be rapidly adapted, 2) have high patient compliance with simple and non-invasive administration, and 3) block transmission following virus challenge. We describe the characterization of an updated single-cycle SARS-CoV-2 vaccine candidate (scVac), engineered as a replication-defective virus with targeted deletions of the E gene and ORF6 and ORF7a, together with a truncation of ORF3a. The candidate carries an Omicron XBB.1.5 Spike (scVac XBB ), while maintaining all essential antigenic properties. Safety was evaluated in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, the most sensitive virulence model, and immunogenicity and efficacy were assessed in the Syrian hamster model. The vaccine was well tolerated in K18-hACE2 transgenic mice, with no clinical signs or adverse events observed. In Syrian hamsters, scVac XBB induced potent systemic and mucosal immune responses, together with a strong neutralising antibody response. Notably, no virus transmission to co-housed naïve animals was detected in the scVac-vaccinated group. In contrast, transmission was observed in the bivalent Omicron mRNA vaccine comparator group under the conditions tested. Our results demonstrate that scVac XBB -induced immunity not only prevents disease but also transmission in a prime-boost hamster direct-contact model following homologous XBB.1.5 challenge. Furthermore, the successful incorporation of the XBB.1.5 Spike protein into the scVac frame supports its potential for adaptation to emerging variants. These findings highlight the potential of this single-cycle vaccine concept as a next-generation COVID-19 vaccine, offering robust protection, effective interruption of transmission, and a favourable tolerability observed in the evaluated animal models. Research was funded by the German Research Foundation, an Innosuisse grant, and by RocketVax AG.

papers.title: Genomic characterization of a novel WVMV isolate and development of a sensitive, field-deployable RT-RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a lateral flow detection assay.
papers.abstract: Wisteria vein mosaic virus (WVMV), a potyviral pathogen, severely compromises the ornamental quality of wisteria plants, yet conventional diagnostic tools fail to support rapid on-site screening under field conditions. Herein, we characterized a novel WVMV isolate designated WVMV-GZWf, recovered from symptomatic wisteria foliage in Guizhou Province, China. Using its full genomic sequence as a reference, we developed a visual molecular diagnostic assay integrating reverse transcription recombinase polymerase amplification (RT-RPA) and CRISPR/Cas12a collateral cleavage. Single-variable gradient assays were performed to optimize core reaction components, yielding optimal concentrations of 10 nM crRNA, 12.5 nM LbCas12a and 400 nM ssDNA-FQ reporter. The established assay achieved a limit of detection (LOD) of 1.55 copies μL⁻¹, corresponding to a 105-fold higher sensitivity than standard RT-PCR. No cross-reactivity was detected against five prevalent plant viruses: potato virus Y, tobacco vein banding mosaic virus, chilli veinal mottle virus, sugarcane mosaic virus and cucumber mosaic virus. The complete workflow takes less than 1 h, with readouts obtainable via portable UV transilluminators or disposable lateral flow dipsticks (LFDs). Testing of field-collected wisteria leaf samples generated diagnostic results fully concordant with RT-PCR. Overall, our RT-RPA-CRISPR/Cas12a-LFD platform enables sensitive, specific and operationally straightforward point-of-care detection of WVMV for field surveillance.

papers.title: Occurrence of tomato brown rugose fruit virus infecting field tomato ( Solanum lycopersicum ) in Hawaii.
papers.abstract: In this short communication, we describe the occurrence of the emerging tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV, Tobamovirus fructirugosum) in Hawaii. Disease and pathogen surveys conducted across the state focusing primarily on field tomato production reveal the presence of ToBRFV in multiple islands, and consistent detection of the virus for several years at the same field suggests it can persist in the field. To our knowledge, this is not only the first report of ToBRFV in Hawaii, but also the first official report of its presence in commercial field for tomato production in the U.S. Analysis of Sanger sequencing data reveal a high identity (>99.4%) between the detected virus isolates and ToBRFV genome sequences reported in the database. Considering the devastating impact of the virus on tomato production, we will work with growers to identify the source of the virus infection and develop practical management strategies to mitigate its impact.

papers.title: Multiplex TaqMan qPCR assay for the rapid detection of Echinococcus spp. in the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
papers.abstract: The co-endemicity of multiple Echinococcus species poses major challenges for accurate pathogen detection and standardized echinococcosis surveillance and control, particularly on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. Nevertheless, conventional molecular detection methods rely on cumbersome conventional and nested polymerase chain reaction (PCR) combinations, which suffer from low detection efficiency, high contamination risks, limited capacity for single-tube multi-species identification, and poor repeatability for low-parasite-load samples, resulting in the absence of standardized, field-applicable detection systems for echinococcosis. To address these limitations, this study developed and validated a novel multiple TaqMan quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) assay based on a lyophilized pre-mixed one-step PCR system for simultaneous identification of three dominant pathogenic Echinococcus species (Echinococcus granulosus s.s., E. multilocularis, and E. shiquicus) in a single reaction. The assay showed excellent analytical performance, including high specificity, excellent linearity, and a low limit of detection of 400 copies/mL. Validation with confirmed samples showed sensitivity of 93.44% and specificity of 100%, significantly superior to conventional combined PCR assays with 67.21% sensitivity. It stably detected trace Echinococcus DNA in complex heterogeneous field samples such as feces from definitive hosts and tiny atypical lesions from intermediate hosts, and accurately identified mixed multi-species infections. Featuring a simplified workflow, low contamination risk, high reproducibility, and suitability for standardization, the developed lyophilized multiplex qPCR system provides a robust technical tool for high-throughput epidemiological surveillance, precise pathogen tracing, and differential diagnosis of echinococcosis in high-altitude endemic regions.

papers.title: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Summit on Genetics in Kidney Health: A United States Perspective.
papers.abstract: Genetic testing and genomics are now essential components of precision kidney care, with the potential to inform diagnosis, management, family planning, and transplant decisions. Expansion of genetic testing is increasingly feasible with continuing improvements in diagnostic yield and variant interpretation as well as declining costs. The Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Genetics in Kidney Health Summit convened experts in nephrology, genetics, genetic counseling, and related disciplines, together with patients and caregivers, to identify strategies for incorporating genetic testing more fully into kidney care in the United States. Patients and caregivers described genetic testing as a possible means of obtaining clarity about the cause of disease, even when treatment options are limited, and of informing reproductive decisions and cascade testing in at-risk relatives. Reflecting these perspectives, summit participants discussed a shift from criteria-based selection toward a more inclusive testing strategy, reframing the question "who should be tested?" to "who should not be tested?" To avoid exclusion of patients who could benefit from genetic testing, testing strategies should be broad and inclusive, potentially approaching universal testing within key clinical contexts, such as early-onset disease, atypical clinical features, family history of CKD, CKD of unexplained cause, or the presence of extrarenal manifestations. To address the current shortage of experts in nephrogenetics and genetic counselors, collaboration of major American nephrology and genetics organizations is needed to enhance kidney genetics training for both trainees and practicing clinicians. Centers of excellence, which at minimum should include a nephrologist with demonstrated expertise in genetic kidney diseases, at least one genetic counselor, and access to accredited laboratories and bioinformatics, can provide guidance to community nephrologists through telemedicine, virtual case discussions, and shared protocols.

papers.title: Diseases causing nervous signs in cattle in South America.
papers.abstract: Neurological diseases in cattle are among the most important diagnostic challenges in veterinary practice and diagnostic laboratories. In South America, surveillance systems and diagnostic networks have progressively expanded the recognition of diseases causing nervous signs in cattle, yet available information remains fragmented across countries. This review integrates current knowledge on the main diseases causing nervous signs in cattle in South America, with emphasis on their clinical presentation, etiopathogenesis, pathology, and diagnostic relevance, and includes brief information on treatment, control, and prevention. For practical purposes, bovine neurologic disorders are organized according to their etiologic origin into infectious, parasitic, toxic, metabolic, neoplastic, and genetic or congenital. Among infectious conditions, rabies remains the most important viral encephalitis in the region, while bovine herpesviral meningoencephalitis, malignant catarrhal fever, listeriosis, thrombotic meningoencephalitis, and suppurative bacterial infections are also relevant differential diagnoses. Parasitic disorders such as cerebral babesiosis, Trypanosoma vivax infection, nervous coccidiosis, neosporosis, coenurosis, and amoebic meningoencephalitis are less frequent but regionally significant. Toxic and metabolic causes are highly diverse and include plant and fungal intoxications, pesticide and lead poisoning, polioencephalomalacia, hypomagnesemia, vitamin A deficiency, ketosis/fatty liver syndrome, and hypocalcemia. Less common but clinically important conditions include nervous system neoplasms and congenital or hereditary disorders. A single integrated table summarizes, for each condition, the etiologic agent, geographic distribution, affected age group and neurolocalization, main neurological syndrome, principal lesions, field diagnostic aids, samples for laboratory confirmation, laboratory diagnostic methods, and the available treatment and control measures. This review highlights the wide etiologic spectrum of bovine diseases causing nervous signs in South America and emphasizes the importance of a systematic diagnostic approach integrating epidemiology, clinical neurology, gross pathology, histopathology, and targeted ancillary tests. A better understanding of these conditions should improve differential diagnosis, therapeutic decision-making, surveillance, and preventive strategies in cattle production systems across the region.

papers.title: Thermodynamically Guided CRISPR Spacer Optimization: Strategy-Dependent Off-Target Trade-Offs.
papers.abstract: Most CRISPR-Cas9 design tools select guide RNAs (gRNAs) by ranking predefined candidates rather than actively optimizing them. Here we instead formulate SpCas9 spacer refinement as a constrained search problem, in which a limited number of nucleotide substitutions may be introduced outside the PAM-proximal seed region. The search is driven by a thermodynamically grounded objective that combines CRISPRspec-based specificity with penalties for suboptimal GC content and long homopolymer runs. Within this single setting we compare five search strategies: three reinforcement-learning (RL) policies, which are Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), Quantile-Regression Deep Q-Network (QR-DQN), and Rainbow Deep Q-Network (Rainbow DQN), together with a nonlearning score-guided search and a prompt-guided large language model (LLM). All five share the same objective, mutable positions, substitution budget, and evaluation protocol, so that only the search strategy differs. On 100 held-out IGF2R guides from a gene and chromosome excluded from training, every strategy significantly reduced the predicted off-target burden (38.6-78.3%) and improved independent specificity metrics without degrading on-target scores. The strategies nevertheless differed sharply in per-guide safety: the LLM achieved the largest aggregate reduction but introduced new off-target sites into 38% of guides that were initially free of them, whereas PPO, an on-policy RL algorithm, retained a strong gain with the lowest regression rate of 15%. These results show that the thermodynamic objective supplies a robust common optimization signal, while the choice of search strategy governs the trade-off between aggregate improvement and regression of already-favorable guides.

papers.title: DeepMolVir: Learning Virtual Virus Representations for Sequence-Aware Virus-Inhibitor Activity Prediction.
papers.abstract: The growing threat of emerging and drug-resistant viruses demands efficient approaches for predicting virus-inhibitor interactions. However, most existing computational models treat viruses as categorical identifiers and fail to capture sequence-level biological information. Here, we assembled a data set of 50,711 compound-virus activity pairs spanning 178 viral species and explored protein language models as a strategy for viral representation learning. Using embeddings generated by ESMC-600M, we introduce a virtual virus representation in which viruses are encoded as sequence-derived biological entities rather than as taxonomic labels. These viral representations are integrated with molecular features to model compound-virus interactions. In extensive 5-fold cross-validation, DeepMolVir demonstrated strong predictive performance, achieving an AUC of 0.8653 and an RMSE of 0.9480. Notably, virtual virus representations consistently outperformed conventional taxonomy-based encodings, while ablation studies highlighted viral sequence information as a key contributor to the model performance. Case studies on Nipah virus and hantaviruses further demonstrated the ability of DeepMolVir to identify candidate antiviral scaffolds and support cross-family drug repurposing. Collectively, our findings establish protein-language-model-based viral representation learning as an effective strategy for sequence-aware antiviral activity prediction and provide a foundation for computational antiviral discovery. Code and data are available at GitHub: https://github.com/Sunny-RPX/DeepMolVir.

papers.title: Structural and biochemical insights into infectious bronchitis virus endoribonuclease Nsp15.
papers.abstract: RNA viruses are not only a human health concern but also an economic concern due to animal infections in major industries. Nsp15, a uridine-specific endoribonuclease conserved across vertebrate nidoviruses, processes viral RNA to evade detection by the host immune system. While the enzymatic function is conserved, the oligomeric state necessary for activity does not appear to be strictly conserved across nidoviruses. How oligomerization affects Nsp15 RNA recognition and processing remains understudied. Here, we report the first cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) structure of a γ-coronavirus Nsp15, using infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a major poultry pathogen, as a model γ-coronavirus. The structure was determined at 2.4 Å resolution and reveals that IBV Nsp15 adopts the characteristic hexameric architecture observed in α- and β-coronavirus Nsp15, including HCoV-229E, SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and MHV. To investigate IBV Nsp15 substrate specificity, we performed endoribonuclease assays using diverse RNA substrates. Despite the high degree of conserved structure, we used Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) to show that IBV Nsp15 exhibits distinct substrate preferences for the nucleotide adjacent to the cleavage site, though this preference does appear to be context-dependent when using more complicated substrates. We also demonstrate that, while not essential for catalysis, divalent metal ions enhance endoribonuclease activity. Collectively, these findings establish the structural and functional framework for γ-coronavirus Nsp15 activity, uncover differences in RNA substrate specificity, and highlight conserved and divergent features of Nsp15 across different nidoviruses that could be utilized for the development of new antiviral targets.IMPORTANCEInfectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a γ-coronavirus, is a major poultry pathogen that encodes an endoribonuclease conserved across coronaviruses. While its enzymatic function is conserved, assembly differs across the viral family. Structural studies revealed that the IBV endoribonuclease assembles into a hexameric structure much like other coronaviruses, yet Förster resonance energy transfer assays demonstrated a sequence preference for the nucleotide 5' to the cleaved base that has not been observed with previous homologs. Additionally, we found that metal ions can boost endoribonuclease activity but are not strictly required. These findings establish a structural and biochemical framework of the IBV endoribonuclease and expand our knowledge of the enzyme across coronaviruses.

papers.title: Applying pharmacogenetic results from cancer genomic tests to advance precision oncology.
papers.abstract: Precision oncology has largely centered on somatic tumor alterations that inform treatment selection, while germline pharmacogenetic information remains underused despite its relevance to anticancer drug safety, dosing, and supportive care. As cancer genomic tests increasingly return pharmacogenetic results, providers must be aware of these results and understand how to interpret and apply these findings in routine practice. This minireview describes key considerations for using pharmacogenetic results generated through cancer genomic tests, including the scope of reported pharmacogenes from various cancer genomics laboratory vendors, clinical actionability of the findings, variant or allele coverage, specimen requirements, and integration of results into clinical workflows. Oncology-relevant pharmacogenes such as DPYD, UGT1A1, TPMT/NUDT15, CYP2D6, and HLA-B*57:01 may inform therapy with fluoropyrimidines, irinotecan, thiopurines, tamoxifen, targeted agents, and supportive care medications. However, vendor platforms differ substantially in gene inclusion, variant/allele coverage, ordering processes, specimen needs, and whether results are returned automatically or by request. Thoughtful integration of pharmacogenetic results can help oncology teams prevent toxicity, optimize treatment, and fully leverage genomic testing in precision cancer care.

papers.title: Integrated functional, structural, and clinical analyses resolve NLRC4 variant pathogenicity in autoinflammatory disease.
papers.abstract: NLRC4-associated autoinflammatory disease (NLRC4-AID) is a rare disorder in which variant interpretation remains challenging because of limited functional evidence. We performed the largest systematic functional characterization of NLRC4 variants to date, assessing 27 mosaic and germline variants, including four identified in our patient cohort. NLRC4 variants were evaluated for their ability to induce inflammasome and NF-κB activation in cells expressing inflammasome components. Functional findings were integrated with structural mapping and clinical evidence and interpreted according to American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) criteria. All mosaic variants exhibited constitutive gain-of-function activity, whereas only 10 of the 22 germline variants displayed increased functional activity. Functionally activating variants clustered near the ADP-binding site and within the leucine-rich repeat domain, regions critical for nucleotide sensing and maintenance of the autoinhibited state. Overall, 15 activating variants were identified in 37 patients from 20 unrelated families. Childhood-onset disease was associated with germline variants or high-level mosaicism, whereas adult-onset disease predominated in low-level mosaicism. All currently reported mosaic variants fulfilled ACMG criteria for pathogenicity, whereas germline variants exhibited marked functional heterogeneity. Integrating functional, structural, and clinical evidence improves NLRC4 variant interpretation, refines ACMG classification, and supports genotype-informed diagnosis and clinical management.

papers.title: Pathway-specific control of keratinocyte mitochondrial energetic dysfunction improves epidermal homeostasis in chronic inflammatory dermatoses.
papers.abstract: Chronic inflammatory dermatoses involve barrier disruption and metabolic dysfunction, yet keratinocyte mitochondrial regulation remains unclear. This study proposes a framework restoring mitochondrial homeostasis via pathway-specific modulation of AMPK, mTOR, and ROS cascades. An in silico model using HaCaT and NHEK datasets simulated interventions affecting redox balance and ATP production. Demonstrate that AMPK-mTOR regulation improves bioenergetics, reduces oxidative stress, and enhances keratinocyte proliferation better than conventional anti-inflammatory approaches. The framework successfully achieved ATP levels of 3.79 mol/g protein, reduced ROS to 38.6%, increased AMPK activation to 0.85, enhanced mTOR activity to 3.6 units, improved keratinocyte proliferation to 89.7, and elevated cytokine expression to 75.9 pg/mL. Overall, pathway-specific modulation provides superior long-term epidermal homeostasis by simultaneously targeting cellular metabolism, redox balance, and differentiation pathways, presenting a robust computational foundation for treating chronic inflammatory skin conditions.

papers.title: Genetic Diagnoses in an Adult Cohort of Predominantly Antibody Deficiency in Australia.
papers.abstract: Predominantly antibody deficiencies (PAD) are the most common IEI. Despite advances in genomics, the diagnostic yield in adults remains below 40%, leaving most patients without a molecular diagnosis to guide clinical management. We aimed to define the spectrum of causative genetic variants in adult PAD patients. 112 adult PAD patients were subjected to whole-exome sequencing, alongside collection of clinical data including serum Ig levels and absolute B and T cell counts. The median age of the cohort was 47 years (range 18-72), and 57% were female. Most patients had common variable immunodeficiency (CVID) (58%), followed by hypogammaglobulinemia (20%), agammaglobulinemia (9%), specific antibody deficiency (10%), and IgG subclass deficiency (4%). Reduced serum IgG, IgA, and IgM levels were observed in 61%, 65%, and 46% of patients, respectively, while low B and T cell counts were present in 35% and 29% of patients. Likely causative or candidate variants were identified in 34 patients (30%). Nine of ten agammaglobulinemia patients harboured BTK variants, with a structural variant in SPI1 identified in the remaining patient. Among the remaining patients, variants were predominantly heterozygous (67%), followed by compound heterozygous (21%) and homozygous (13%). Variants most commonly affected genes involved in B cell differentiation and signalling (BTK, NFKB1, PIK3R1, PLCG2, and SYK; 44%), followed by CTLA-4 recycling (CTLA, LRBA; 9%) and TACI receptor (TNFRSF13B; 24%). This first report of an Australian adult PAD cohort demonstrates genetic diagnosis rates consistent with international studies and highlights substantial genetic heterogeneity. Using in-house assays, we are currently functionally validating this diverse array of variants.

papers.title: Determinants of DNA-sequence-based Diagnostic Yield in the CSER Consortium.
papers.abstract: Diagnostic yield from exome and genome sequencing varies widely across studies. It remains unclear how much of this variation reflects patient-level factors (e.g., sex, clinical features, race/ethnicity, genetic ancestry) versus site-level practices such as sequencing modality or variant interpretation workflows. We aimed to quantify the contributions of these factors to diagnostic outcomes across five U.S. clinical sequencing sites. We performed a cross-sectional analysis of 3,008 prenatal, neonatal, and pediatric cases from the NHGRI Clinical Sequencing Evidence-Generating Research (CSER) consortium (2017-2023). Clinical indications spanned neurodevelopmental, neurological, immunological, metabolic, craniofacial, skeletal, cardiac, prenatal, and oncologic presentations. Genetic ancestry was inferred from sequencing data, and variants were interpreted using ACMG/AMP guidelines to classify DNA-based diagnoses. Generalized linear mixed models were used to estimate associations between diagnostic yield and fixed effects (sex, prenatal status, isolated cancer, number of clinical indications, sequencing modality, race/ethnicity, and genetic ancestry), while modeling study site as a random effect to quantify between-site variation. The overall diagnostic yield was 19.0%. Multiple clinical indications (OR=1.47, 95% CI 1.20-1.80, p<0.001) were associated with higher diagnostic yield, and male sex (OR=0.80, 95% CI 0.66-0.96, p=0.017) and prenatal status (OR=0.63, 95% CI 0.44-0.90, p=0.012) were associated with lower yield. Sequencing modality, race/ethnicity, genetic ancestry, and isolated cancer were not statistically significantly associated with diagnostic outcomes. A model without fixed effects attributed ∼10% of variance in diagnostic yield to between-site differences. After adjusting for covariates, site-level variance decreased to 5.7%, indicating consistent variation across sites not explained by measured patient factors. Across five sites, patient-level clinical features influenced diagnostic yield, but substantial site-level variation remained even after adjustment. Differences in variant interpretation, or case-classification practices may contribute to this residual variability. Further efforts to increase consistency in exome- and genome-sequencing diagnostic workflows may help reduce inter-site differences.

papers.title: Bioinspired Membrane Fusion-Gated Hydrogel Biosensor for Extraction-Free Viral RNA Detection of Infectious Influenza Virus.
papers.abstract: Emerging infectious diseases driven by zoonotic spillover demand rapid and reliable molecular diagnostics for pathogen identification and surveillance. However, conventional nucleic acid diagnostics cannot distinguish infectious virions from nonviable RNA fragments, limiting infectivity-resolved virus identification. Here, we report a bioinspired membrane-coated hydrogel (Memgel) sensor that enables extraction-free molecular detection of influenza virus while distinguishing fusion-competent virions from noninfectious viral material. The platform integrates a cell-mimetic supported lipid bilayer with a polyethylene glycol diacrylate (PEGDA) hydrogel matrix encapsulating recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) reagents. Under endosome-mimicking acidic conditions, hemagglutinin-mediated membrane fusion selectively delivers viral genomic RNA from infectious virions into the hydrogel matrix, triggering sequence-specific amplification while suppressing signals from free viral RNA fragments. As a proof of concept, the Memgel sensor was evaluated for the detection of influenza A (H9N2) in simulated nasal fluid and raw milk matrices, achieving a limit of detection of 10 1.23 TCID 50 mL - 1 while maintaining robust detection performance without RNA extraction. Coupled with a portable fluorescence reader, the system demonstrates compatibility with compact fluorescence-based readout for future point-of-care implementation. This fusion-gated sensing strategy provides a materials-based framework for infectivity-resolved molecular diagnostics of emerging viral pathogens.

papers.title: The Therapeutic Pipeline: Future Treatments and Precision Medicine.
papers.abstract: Rare interstitial lung diseases (ILDs) represent a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by various pathogenic mechanisms, clinical presentations, prognoses, and therapeutic challenges. Among these, acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (ASMD), pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis (PLCH) exemplify rare pulmonary diseases driven by distinct biological mechanisms, including lysosomal dysfunction, impaired surfactant homeostasis, and activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK) pathways. Recent advancements in molecular biology, genomics, and translational research boosted the development of precision medicine strategies and disease-specific therapies for these conditions. This narrative review was conducted in accordance with the SANRA guidelines. A thorough literature search of the PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, and Scopus databases was performed from January 2000 to June 2026. Significant progress has been made in treating all three diseases. In ASMD, enzyme replacement therapy with olipudase alfa has greatly improved visceral and lung symptoms, while research in gene therapy, gene editing, and metabolic treatments is ongoing. For PAP, inhaled granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) is now the primary disease-specific treatment, now supported by phase III trial evidence for inhaled molgramostim, complemented by potential therapies such as immunomodulation, macrophage transplantation, and gene-based strategies. In PLCH, the discovery of recurrent MAPK pathway variants has supported the use of genotype-targeted treatments with B-Raf proto-oncogene, serine (BRAF)/threonine kinase and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) kinase inhibitors. Under these conditions, advances in molecular diagnostics, circulating biomarkers, quantitative high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT), radiomics, and artificial intelligence (AI) are poised to enhance diagnosis, patient stratification, prognosis, and treatment decisions. ASMD, PAP, and PLCH are entering into an era of precision medicine, in which disease-specific molecular mechanisms play an increasing role in guiding diagnosis and treatment. Ongoing integration of genomics, biomarkers, advanced imaging, AI, and targeted therapies could revolutionize the management of conditions such as ASMD, PAP, and PLCH, leading to better long-term patient outcomes.

papers.title: Evolving roles within the genomic medicine workforce: a revised framework for UK practice-position on behalf of the Association of Genetic Nurses and Counsellors and the Clinical Genetics Society.
Serological Evidence of Exposure to Crimean-Congo Hemorrhagic Fever Virus in Equids in Spain.
papers.abstract: Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (CCHFV) is an emerging tick-borne zoonotic pathogen in western Europe, with established circulation in Spain. Although wildlife hosts are known to contribute to virus maintenance, the role of domestic species, including equids, remains poorly understood. This study aimed to assess serological reactivity against CCHFV in equids in endemic regions of Spain. A total of 494 equids, including 430 horses (Equus caballus), 54 mules (Equus mulus) and 10 donkeys (Equus asinus) were analyzed. Samples were screened with a commercial double-antigen multispecies ELISA and all ELISA-reactive sera, together with a subset of ELISA-negative sera, were tested by virus neutralization test (VNT). Eleven of 494 animals were ELISA-reactive (apparent ELISA seroprevalence 2.2%; 95% CI: 1.1-3.9), comprising 7 horses (1.6%; 95% CI: 0.7-3.3) and 4 mules (7.4%; 95% CI: 2.1-17.9); no reactive donkeys were detected (0%; 95% CI: 0-30.8). Reactive animals originated exclusively from Andalucía (10/184; 5.4%) and Castilla-La Mancha (1/90; 1.1%). None of the 11 ELISA-reactive sera showed detectable neutralizing antibodies (titers < 1:8). While these findings suggest potential CCHFV exposure, the opportunistic sampling and VNT-negative results indicate that this 2.2% rate represents apparent ELISA reactivity rather than a true seroprevalence. Consequently, further studies incorporating molecular detection and validated neutralization assays are required to definitively confirm virus circulation in Spanish equid populations.

papers.title: Primer-programmed circular template generation enables padlock-free rolling circle amplification for low-background CRISPR-based pathogen detection.
papers.abstract: Rolling circle amplification (RCA) is a powerful nucleic acid amplification strategy, yet conventional RCA-based biosensing often relies on target-specific padlock probes for circular template construction, which increases probe-design complexity and may introduce nonspecific ligation and background amplification. Here, we develop a padlock-free RCA strategy for CRISPR-based pathogen detection through primer-programmed circular template generation (PPCTG) strategy. Asymmetric recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) with rationally designed phosphorylated primers generates target-derived single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), which subsequently undergoes universal splint-mediated circularization to form amplification templates without target-specific padlock probes. By integrating target recognition into the amplification-derived ssDNA intermediate, PPCTG couples target amplification with circular template generation while simplifying probe design and reducing nonspecific background. The resulting circular templates support continuous RCA, generating long ssDNA scaffolds that provide abundant activator sites for CRISPR-Cas12a, thereby enabling cascaded signal amplification through trans-cleavage of fluorophore-quencher reporters. The platform achieved a limit of detection of 3.47 aM for Staphylococcus aureus with high analytical specificity. Moreover, extraction-free detection was demonstrated in crude sputum and exhaled breath condensate, with recovery rates of 96.4%-105.5% and good agreement with qPCR results. Overall, PPCTG provides a padlock-free strategy for programmable circular template generation and integrates target amplification, RCA, and CRISPR-Cas12a signal amplification into a streamlined workflow, offering a low-background and ultrasensitive approach for pathogen detection in complex biological matrices.

papers.title: Mechanisms and applications of condensed RNA-based molecular crowding on enhancing RNA aptamer performance.
papers.abstract: RNA aptamers represent promising recognition bioreceptors for biosensing, yet practical applications are severely hampered by limited binding affinity, poor thermal stability and high susceptibility to nuclease-mediated degradation. Intracellular molecular crowding environments driven by liquid-liquid phase separation can remodel RNA conformation and improve biomolecular function, inspiring the construction of artificial condensed RNA systems to address the performance bottlenecks of RNA aptamers for foodborne pathogen detection. In this work, we engineered a CUG-trinucleotide-repeat-based condensed RNA platform coordinated with cationic Poly-l-lysine (Poly-L-Lys) to enhance the detection performance of an RNA aptamer targeting Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus), a critical food-contaminating pathogen. Non-hollow RNA condensates with heterogeneous spatial architecture were successfully formed in vitro. Compared with non-condensed aptamers, the condensed RNA achieved 22.04% higher binding affinity, an 11.63% elevated melting temperature, and improved nuclease resistance. Mechanistic investigations revealed that molecular crowding rearranged aptamer secondary-structure, switched binding thermodynamics from entropy-driven to enthalpy-driven, and accelerated target-binding kinetics. After integration into a pH-sensitive colorimetric assay, key analytical performance metrics including sensitivity, linear dynamic range, limit of detection, and reproducibility were comprehensively characterized. The sensor exhibited a sensitivity of 0.06 absorbance per log 10 (CFU·mL -1 ), a linear dynamic range spanning 10 2 -10 8 CFU mL -1 , with a limit of detection of 236 ± 43 CFU mL -1 . Satisfactory assay selectivity, good reproducibility, and acceptable recoveries ranging from 80% to 120% were achieved across multiple complex food matrices including pork, oilseed rape, milk and apple juice. This work establishes a feasible molecular crowding engineering strategy for boosting RNA aptamer performance. The condensed RNA sensing platform provides a reliable analytical tool for food-safety monitoring and opens new avenues for designing next-generation nucleic-acid-based biosensors.

papers.title: Chromosomal Amplification in Pediatric Tumors: Implications and Therapeutic Strategies.
papers.abstract: Pediatric tumors often exhibit relatively low coding mutation burdens, and recurrent chromosomal amplifications are observed in specific tumor entities. These amplifications may contribute to influence tumor initiation, progression, and treatment response. For instance, amplification of the MYCN oncogene is a well-established marker of high-risk neuroblastoma and is associated with aggressive disease and poor outcomes. Advances in genomics and molecular biology have identified numerous chromosomal amplification events in pediatric tumors and provided insights into their underlying mechanisms. In this review, we first examine the molecular mechanisms driving chromosomal amplification. We then discuss the roles of chromosomal amplifications in pediatric tumorigenesis and summarize therapeutic approaches, including targeted inhibition, combination strategies, and experimental approaches to promote oncoprotein degradation. Throughout, we distinguish promising therapeutic concepts and preclinical findings from strategies with demonstrated clinical benefit. Further Integration of mechanistic studies, functional validation and biomarker-guided clinical trails may help advance precision therapy for pediatric tumors.

papers.title: Genomic insights into Clostridium perfringens from diverse animals: phylogeny, toxinotypes, and CAZyme profiles.
papers.abstract: Clostridium perfringens is a significant pathogen affecting both human and animal health, yet comprehensive cross-host comparative studies are lacking. This study aimed to characterize the phenotypic and genomic features of C. perfringens isolates from diverse animal hosts. A total of 77 isolates were obtained from 665 samples of dairy cattle, chickens, sheep, horses, cats, and deer, including both healthy and diarrheic individuals. Hemolytic assay was conducted to evaluate the hemolytic capabilities. Whole-genome sequencing was performed on 29 representative isolates. Phylogenetic relationships were reconstructed based on core-genome SNPs, and virulence factor profiles were determined. Carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) were annotated to assess potential differences in mucosal colonization capabilities. Isolation rates were significantly higher in diarrheic animals compared to healthy counterparts. Hemolytic assay revealed that isolates from diarrheic animals generally exhibited greater hemolytic capabilities, with sheep-derived strains showing the highest activity. Phylogenomic analysis demonstrated distinct host-associated clustering, although specific virulent lineages clustered together, suggesting potential for cross-species transmission. Toxinotyping identified 24 type A, 4 type D (exclusively from diarrheic sheep), and 1 type E (from diarrheic deer) isolates. Comparative genomics revealed a uniquely enriched CAZyme repertoire in the highly virulent sheep isolates, specifically enriched in glycoside hydrolases (GH89, GH98), carbohydrate-binding modules (CBM40, CBM51), and polysaccharide lyases (PL8), indicating enhanced capacity for mucosal adhesion and degradation. This multi-host study provides novel insights into the genomic landscape of C. perfringens, highlighting that host-specific evolution is accompanied by distinct virulence potentials. These findings provide a scientific basis for developing targeted surveillance and control strategies in veterinary practice.

papers.title: From Technical Performance to Clinical Impact: Challenges and Opportunities for AI Modelling of CKD Progression.
papers.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a major global health burden, with highly heterogeneous trajectories ranging from long-term stability to rapid progression towards kidney failure and kidney replacement therapy. Accurate prediction of CKD progression is essential to support personalised monitoring, timely therapeutic intensification, nephrology referral, and preparation for advanced kidney care. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) approaches may improve risk stratification by modelling complex, nonlinear, and time-dependent patterns in routinely collected clinical data, electronic health records, and potentially multimodal data sources. Nonetheless, it remains unclear how ready these AI-driven models are for clinical use. This structured narrative review aimed to map the current landscape of AI for predicting CKD progression, assess the robustness and clinical relevance of the evidence, and identify methodological and implementation gaps that must be addressed to translate technical accuracy into clinical impact. This review synthesised 35 studies published between 2020 and 2025 that developed and evaluated models to predict CKD progression. Most studies used retrospective cohort designs and electronic health record data, relying mainly on demographic variables, laboratory measures, comorbidities, and clinical history. Tree-based models, random forests, boosting methods, regression-based approaches, and neural networks were the most commonly investigated methods. Overall, the reviewed models often achieved favourable discriminative performance, as measured by AUROC or C-index. Nevertheless, the evidence base remains limited by substantial heterogeneity in study designs, cohort compositions, prediction targets, time horizons, feature engineering, and validation strategies. External validation was reported in only about one-quarter of studies, while calibration, clinical utility, patient-level uncertainty, and implementation-oriented evaluation were inconsistently addressed. Prediction endpoints were predominantly kidney failure-related. Multimodal data, including imaging, genomics, and social determinants of health, were rarely used, and explainability methods were more often applied for model description than for clinician-facing decision support. AI models show substantial promise for predicting CKD progression, particularly when trained on routinely available clinical data. However, the field remains more advanced in model development than in clinical validation and implementation. Future research should prioritise external and temporal validation, systematic calibration assessment, decision-curve or net-benefit analysis, comparison with established clinical risk scores, clinically meaningful prediction horizons, subgroup and fairness evaluation, patient-level uncertainty estimation, and prospective testing of model-informed care. These steps are essential to move from statistically accurate models to reliable, interpretable, equitable, and actionable tools for CKD management.

papers.title: MicroBioAgent: an AI agent for automated microbiome analysis
papers.abstract: Microbiome data analysis demands customized workflows tailored to specific biological questions, sequencing modalities, and data properties. However, constructing and executing these workflows requires navigating heterogeneous software dependencies, reference databases, and multi-step parameter tuning. Here, we present MicroBioAgent, an autonomous, domain-specific agent framework that translates high-level biological queries into executable, study-specific pipelines across 16S rRNA amplicon, reference-based shotgun, and de novo assembly-based metagenomics. Rather than relying on static pipeline templates, MicroBioAgent employs a closed-loop execution architecture: it dynamically selects and runs bioinformatics tools within user-controlled environments while iteratively inspecting intermediate outputs to adapt downstream analytical decisions. Furthermore, to address the long-running nature of metagenomic computation, we introduce an asynchronous background task-management mechanism that reduces LLM token consumption by over 50% while enabling real-time plan adjustment and automated workflow resumption. We systematically evaluated MicroBioAgent across three benchmarks of increasing complexity: (1) paired amplicon and shotgun profiling of tomato rhizosphere microbiomes, (2) taxonomic and functional profiling coupled with machine-learning classification in a colorectal cancer cohort, and (3) de novo metagenomic assembly, metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) binning, and metabolic pathway reconstruction in a polyethylene degradation study. Across all benchmarks, MicroBioAgent faithfully recapitulated the primary biological findings of the original studies, exhibiting high analytical concordance despite expected tool- and database-dependent variations. In systematic robustness evaluations across 27 independent runs spanning three backbone large language models and three prompt-complexity tiers, MicroBioAgent achieved a 98.8% task completion rate and yielded highly reproducible diversity and differential-abundance estimates. MicroBioAgent establishes a scalable, adaptive paradigm for end-to-end computational microbiome research.

papers.title: Syngeneic human iPSC Macrophages and Microglia possess distinct neuroinflammatory profiles, responses to HIV infection, and ART treatment
papers.abstract: Macrophages are innate immune cells that primarily function as professional phagocytes, playing essential roles throughout the body in host defense and maintaining homeostasis. The CNS is populated by two anatomically distinct macrophage populations; parenchymal microglia and border-resident CNS-associated macrophages (CAMs). These populations coordinate the neuroinflammatory response to pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) through Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling and are exposed to distinct microenvironmental cues that could shape their functions. CNS macrophages are also involved in infection with neurotropic viruses such as HIV, where the persistent infection contributes to chronic neuroinflammation and the constellation of other neurological symptoms collectively termed neuroHIV. Although antiretroviral therapy (cART) has transformed HIV care and lessened the severity of many neuroHIV symptoms, the persistence of CNS viral reservoirs and neurological deficits remains a major comorbidity and barrier to cure. Understanding specific contributions of microglia and CAMs to inflammation and neuroHIV has been challenging due to the lack of genetically matched human model systems enabling direct mechanistic comparison between of microglia and CAMs. To address this, we optimized the generation of syngeneic, human-induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC) derived microglia-like (iMg) and CAM-like (iMacs) cells. These are generated simultaneously from a single donor line and have the same genetic background, enabling side-by-side characterization and functional analyses of inflammation and HIV infection. Transcriptomic profiling by RNA sequencing revealed substantial baseline differences in inflammatory and immune signaling pathways between iMg and iMacs. These intrinsic differences were also observed in TLR-specific NF-{kappa}B responses. Stimulation of TLR4 drove heightened response in iMg relative to iMac, correlating closely with morphological changes, while stimulating TLR2 had a contrasting effect, eliciting a stronger and more robust early NF-{kappa}B response in iMacs. In HIV infection studies, iMacs were more permissive to viral replication at baseline, whereas iMg showed a reduced susceptibility to infection. However, iMacs responded more robustly to cART, while iMg exhibited relative resistance to cART-mediated suppression. These findings delineate fundamental inflammatory and virologic differences between human microglia and CAMs and provide a robust foundation on which to further examine HIV infection, cART efficacy, and immune function in these distinct CNS myeloid populations.

papers.title: Variation of anti-oomycete activity in Pseudomonas spp.: phenotypic characterization and comparative genomics
papers.abstract: Pathogenic aquatic oomycetes Aphanomyces astaci and Saprolegnia parasitica represent a major threat to biodiversity and aquaculture production, but their interactions with host-associated microbes remain poorly understood. From a collection of bacterial isolates (n = 328) obtained from fish and crayfish hosts, we focused on Pseudomonas spp. (n = 66) and confirmed their previously reported strong inhibitory potential against A. astaci and S. parasitica. However, our results also revealed substantial inter- and intra-species variation in antagonism. To capture this variation, we selected eight isolates belonging to different P. fluorescens, P. putida, and P. syringae species groups and displaying contrasting levels of anti-oomycete activity for further phenotypic assays and comparative genomic analysis. Across these isolates, mycelial inhibition was markedly stronger against A. astaci than against S. parasitica, indicating species-specific differences in susceptibility. Comparative genomic analysis revealed substantial variation in biosynthetic gene cluster (BGC) repertoires among the analysed strains. Strongly inhibitory isolates carried candidate BGCs with similarity to characterised bioactive pathways, including pyoluteorin, rhizoxin, pyrrolnitrin, DAPG, and orfamide, alongside with multiple uncharacterised clusters that were either shared among inhibitory isolates or restricted to individual strains. All analysed genomes also contained clusters related to siderophore and HCN biosynthesis. However, in vitro assays showed that siderophore production was not clearly associated with inhibitory activity and that total inhibition was considerably higher than volatile-only inhibition, suggesting a substantial contribution of non-volatile, presumably diffusible, compounds. Altogether, our results suggest that Pseudomonas anti-oomycete activity is species- and strain-dependent and likely reflects different combinations of multiple metabolites, likely including diffusible compounds, rather than a single conserved mechanism. In conclusion, this study provides a foundation for future work aimed at resolving mechanisms underlying microbial antagonism toward aquatic oomycete pathogens.

papers.title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

papers.title: Spatial genomics of the cardiac sarcomere
papers.abstract: Structure-function mapping of proteins has improved our understanding of disease mechanisms and protein domains while human population genetics has provided a window into variational tolerance that can be modeled at a structural level. Here, to reveal novel insight into the cardiac sarcomere, the motor unit of the heart, we develop a novel analytical framework to integrate data from over 17,000 patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) and combine it with two population-scale genomic databases that incorporate data from more than 1.2 million individuals. We integrate in silico genetic predictions of gene variant pathogenicity with 3 dimensional integrative spatial scanning across multiple structural models of cardiac motor proteins. Results reveal both recognized and novel regions of structural variant intolerance across the critical genes of the cardiac sarcomere including novel insights into protein function. We discuss the structural relevance of mutational enrichment in the context of sarcomere organization and destabilization of sequestered myosin leading to hypercontractility seen in HCM, by incorporating the recently defined high-resolution structure of human cardiac myosin filament. We extend and validate these findings through pathogenic variant class enrichment and reveal novel associations with the earlier onset of disease in a large clinical cohort. In summary, our study provides a multi-dimensional framework for integrating structural, genomic, and modeling data to reveal novel insight into the cardiac sarcomere.

papers.title: Prioritizing Maize Metabolic Gene Regulators through Multi-Omic Network Integration
papers.abstract: Transcription factors control all biological processes, yet most remain functionally uncharacterized. As in many crops, maize functional genomics datasets are typically generated independently across genotypes, tissues, and laboratories, with little sample overlap and uneven transcription factor coverage, limiting methods that require matched measurements to make functional inferences. Here, we asked which gene-level integration strategy best predicts transcription factor function from such data. We assembled four transcription factor-target gene network layers from 46 expression-based regulatory networks, 283 protein-DNA interaction assays, and expression quantitative trait loci mapped with 16 million single-nucleotide polymorphisms across 304 inbred lines, comprising ~4.6 million interactions, and benchmarked three integration strategies against published knockout transcriptomes. Predicted Gene Ontology terms were more similar to knockout responses than expected by chance, and summarizing each gene's connectivity pattern across the combined network as a numerical representation (a gene embedding) achieved the highest similarity where predictions existed, annotated more than eightfold more transcription factors (2,910), remained informative when data layers were missing, and produced significant terms in only ~12% of randomized networks, versus ~28% and ~72% for two overlap-based strategies. The resulting catalog recovers known regulators, prioritizes candidate regulators of hormonal, developmental, and metabolic processes across conditions, and identifies candidate redundant or diverged paralogs, providing a first testable function for thousands of transcription factors that lack binding or mutant data. Because it uses only data types now available for many crops, the strategy transfers directly to other plant species.

papers.title: Non-invasive detection of tissue clonal mosaicism in chronic disease
papers.abstract: Liquid biopsy has transformed our ability to non-invasively interrogate the somatic genome, but its reach has been largely confined to fetal genetics in prenatal testing and tumor genetics in cancer. Clonal mosaicism (CM) pervades non-malignant solid tissues, where somatic driver mutations expand under specific selective pressures and may shape the course of chronic illness. Access to this biology has been limited to invasive tissue biopsies, restricting the field to small cohorts and single time points, and has precluded large-scale, clinically-linked analyses. Here, ultra-sensitive cell-free DNA (cfDNA) sequencing of patients with chronic liver disease revealed genome-wide somatic variants from matched liver biopsies at plasma fractions comparable to those of cancers (10^-4 - 10^-5), with signal corresponding to variants from spatially and phylogenetically related clones. A biopsy-naive targeted panel detected pathogenic variants in chronic liver disease driver genes in 81.5% patients with chronic liver disease, undetectable in controls, with stage-specific enrichment of ACVR2A in early disease and clearance of liver-derived signal following transplant. Extending the framework to inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), we detect clonal expansions of IBD driver genes in active ulcerative colitis, and observe greater detection in patients with pancolitis versus more localized disease. Together, these results open a new domain for cfDNA genetics beyond cancer and prenatal genetics, the non-invasive interrogation of somatic evolution in chronic disease, and establish a framework for the large-cohort, longitudinal, clinically linked studies of solid-tissue CM that has been inaccessible to the field.

papers.title: Machine learning prediction of antimicrobial resistance in respiratory metagenomes
papers.abstract: Background: Targeted therapy for patients with suspected respiratory infections traditionally requires bacterial culture followed by phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST), a process that can take up to 5 days. In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), delays in identifying the causative pathogen and its resistance profile may be especially harmful because patients are critically ill and often receive broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics. The growing burden of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) further complicates clinical decision-making by reducing effective treatment options and increasing the risk of inadequate initial therapy. Culture-free, AI-driven computational metagenomic strategies have the potential to drastically shorten this window, enabling more rapid targeted therapy prescription. To show the feasibility of such approaches, we develop a proof-of-concept framework based on clinical metagenomics. Methods: We simulated respiratory metagenomes using real-world bacterial genomes with associated antimicrobial susceptibility phenotypes. Each simulated metagenome contained a fixed commensal background and one clinically important respiratory pathogen, Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, or Pseudomonas aeruginosa, at 5% or 10% bacterial read abundance. Realistic reads were simulated for Oxford Nanopore, PacBio, and Illumina sequencing platforms. Random Forest (RF) classifiers were trained and evaluated using five-fold, strain-grouped cross-validation with fold-specific {chi}2-ranked 13-mer features. ResFinder and KARGA were included as reference-based metagenomics benchmarks and evaluated using the same five held-out folds across the three sequencing platforms and two pathogen-abundance conditions. Results: RF performance varied substantially across species, antibiotics, and sequencing platforms. The strongest and most consistent results were observed for K. pneumoniae, with accuracy reaching approximately 0.96 for ceftazidime, 0.93 for amikacin, and 0.92 for ciprofloxacin. Performance for P. aeruginosa was more heterogeneous: long-read models performed well for amikacin, reaching 0.89 with PacBio and 0.88 with Nanopore, whereas Illumina performed substantially better for ciprofloxacin, ceftazidime, and levofloxacin, reaching accuracies of approximately 0.87, 0.77, and 0.70, respectively. Across most organism-antibiotic combinations, RF accuracy was numerically higher than the classification accuracies obtained with KARGA and ResFinder, which generally remained near 0.50. Increasing pathogen abundance from 5% to 10% and increasing the number of selected features from 2,500 to 5,000 generally produced modest improvements in classification accuracy, although the magnitude of improvement varied across organism-antibiotic combinations and sequencing platforms. Conclusions: Genome-wide k-mer machine learning can recover phenotype-associated antimicrobial resistance signals from simulated respiratory metagenomes, although performance depends strongly on the organism, antibiotic, and sequencing platform. These results represent a simulation-based proof of concept.

papers.title: A2Holo: Dual-Stream Flow Matching of 3D Structure and a Protein Language Model for Conformational Transition Prediction
papers.abstract: Modelling a ligand-bound holo conformation from a ligand-free apo conformation is essential in structure-based drug discovery. We present A2Holo, which casts apo-to-holo prediction as flow matching between two experimental structures rather than generation from noise. It transplants the dual-stream joint attention of in-context image generation to residue-aligned protein language model embeddings and structure. Without ligand conditioning or stochastic sampling, A2Holo's single deterministic trajectory reaches a median C RMSD of 0.809 [A] on the D3PM benchmark, the lowest among existing methods. Its TM-score exceeds even the best of 10 samples from every stochastic baseline on at least 144 of 150 pairs. Beyond performance, we directly measure the transplanted multimodal mechanism itself. Because sequence and structure are residue-aligned, its joint attention can be measured at residue resolution and tested for reproducibility across independently trained model variants. Within the structure stream, the attention a residue receives recovers moving residues better than the attention it emits, and this asymmetry is learned. A2Holo demonstrates a successful multimodal transplant from in-context image generation to protein conformational change, with strong deterministic apo-to-holo prediction. It also provides a quantitative account of how that mechanism organises residue-aligned sequence and structure around the residues that move.

papers.title: aureoRNA enables the interactive, genome-wide analysis of Staphylococcus aureus small RNA targetomes and uncovers new regulatory functions
papers.abstract: Small RNAs (sRNAs) control key steps of infection and stress acclimation in the opportunistic pathogen Staphylococcus aureus. Yet most of the more than 250 annotated candidates remain uncharacterized, and even the best-studied have incomplete target spectra. Here we present aureoRNA, an interactive tool that assembles for each sRNA comparative target predictions, available MAPS interactomes, sRNA-mRNA expression correlation across curated public transcriptomes and placement in groups of independently regulated genes (iModulons), and makes these data explorable in one place. GO- and KEGG-based enrichments summarize the datasets at the pathway level for every sRNA, and a weighted rank product combines available data into prioritized target candidate lists. We generated a new MAPS interactome for RsaD and experimentally validated predictions for three sRNAs: new RsaD targets in threonine and arginine catabolism, citZ as an RsaE target, and prophage genes repressed by RNAIII. aureoRNA is a hypothesis-generating resource for the systematic characterization of the sRNA repertoire of this pathogen.

papers.title: The IGVF Catalog Knowledge Graph
papers.abstract: The Impact of Genomic Variation on Function (IGVF) consortium is systematically characterizing how genomic variation influences regulatory elements, gene expression, and human phenotypes through thousands of experimental mapping and perturbation datasets alongside predictive models. To synthesize these diverse results into quantitative relationships and situate them within established biological knowledge, we developed the IGVF Catalog, a large-scale knowledge graph. Implemented in ArangoDB using schema-validated JSON records. Version 1.3 encompasses nearly 3 billion nodes across 14 entity types (including variants, coding variants, genomic elements, genes, transcripts, proteins, pathways, and ontology graphs for biosamples and phenotypes) connected by more than 8.6 billion edges across 31 relationship types. Edges encode statistical significance, effect sizes, source provenance, and biological context via ontology-linked hyperedges. The Catalog integrates 657 IGVF datasets spanning non-coding reporter and CRISPR perturbation screens (MPRA, STARR-seq, Perturb-seq), coding variant assays (VAMP-seq, SGE, MAVE, DUAL-IPA), and predictive models (scE2G, SEMVAR, cV2F, TLAND, and BlueSTARR), unified with extensive public context including GENCODE annotations, FAVOR and dbSNP variants, TopLD linkage disequilibrium, GWAS, QTLs, and protein interactions. Users can interrogate the Catalog through a web portal (https://igvf.catalog.org) Python and R clients, an OpenAPI-documented API featuring 86 endpoints supporting identifier and genomic-region queries, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server enabling agent-assisted querying with large language models. We demonstrate the Catalog's utility for mechanistic interpretation across three case studies: resolving a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant (rs11257655) regulating CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus, distinguishing coding (GCKR rs1260326) and regulatory (HNF1A rs1169289) mechanisms for liver traits, and linking vascular CRISPRi-perturbed elements to CDKN2A/CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease.
